title: Color
summary: Use color to show hierarchy, status, and brand, and keep text readable in both light and dark appearances.
whenToUse: To distinguish a primary action, a selected state, or a status.
To carry a restrained brand accent through the interface.
whenNotToUse: As the only signal for an error, success, or required field.
To decorate large surfaces that compete with content.

rules.statement: Name colors by role, such as label, secondary label, background, separator, accent, and danger, instead of by a raw value.
Keep a single accent for primary actions and selection so people can spot the next step.
Do not style a destructive action with the accent color.
Pair color with text or a symbol whenever the color carries meaning.
On the web, define those roles as custom properties and override the same names under prefers-color-scheme: dark.

cssNotes: Define --color-label, --color-label-secondary, --color-bg, --color-bg-elevated, --color-separator, --color-accent, and --color-danger.
Body copy uses --color-label on --color-bg. Metadata uses --color-label-secondary.
Do not hard-code Apple system-color hex values; they change with appearance and vibrancy.
accessibility: Body text should clear WCAG AA contrast, 4.5:1, and large text or interface components 3:1.
Focus indicators must stay visible on both appearances.

title: Typography
summary: A short type scale creates hierarchy. Let people enlarge the text.
whenToUse: To separate a title, the body, and supporting metadata.
To keep reading comfortable on a phone or a wide column.
whenNotToUse: To invent a new size for every screen.
To shrink text so more content fits.

rules.statement: Use a small set of roles: large title, title, headline, body, callout, subhead, footnote, and caption.
Body is the default. Larger roles are titles. Smaller roles are metadata.
Respect the reader's text-size setting instead of locking a pixel size.
On the web, use the system UI font stack and rem units so browser zoom and user font settings work.
Keep a long-reading line around 60 to 80 characters.

cssNotes: font-family: ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif. Do not bundle or redistribute San Francisco.
A practical web scale: large title 2rem/700, title 1.5rem/700, headline 1.125rem/600, body 1rem/400, subhead 0.9375rem, footnote 0.8125rem, caption 0.75rem.
Body line-height around 1.45. This scale names HIG text roles; it is not Apple's point table.
accessibility: Do not disable zoom or set a maximum scale.
Use rem or the browser default so people can enlarge text.

title: Layout
summary: Align content to a consistent spacing rhythm and keep controls easy to hit as the window changes size.
whenToUse: To place controls, text, and groups on a screen that must adapt.
To decide between a tab bar and a sidebar as width changes.
whenNotToUse: To stretch a phone layout across a wide desktop window with no grouping.

rules.statement: Give every control a hit region of at least 44 by 44 points. On visionOS, aim for 60 points.
Space related items more tightly than unrelated groups, using a 4 or 8 point step.
Keep content out of the safe areas and the home indicator.
On a narrow width, use a tab bar for a few top-level destinations. On a wide width, use a sidebar.
On the web, map safe areas to env(safe-area-inset-*) and let the page reflow instead of scaling the whole layout.

cssNotes: Use a spacing scale of 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, and 32 pixels.
padding: env(safe-area-inset-top) env(safe-area-inset-right) env(safe-area-inset-bottom) env(safe-area-inset-left).
Switch from a bottom navigation bar to a sidebar around 800 pixels of width.
accessibility: Interactive targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, with space between neighbors.
Reading order in the DOM matches the visual order.

title: Materials
summary: Translucency shows what sits behind a bar or sheet. It is a depth cue, not a texture for every surface.
whenToUse: Behind a toolbar, tab bar, or sheet that floats over content.
To separate a foreground control from a busy background.
whenNotToUse: On body content, long text, or stacked panels that each blur the last.

rules.statement: Use at most one or two translucent layers in a view.
Put text on a material only when the fill keeps it readable. Otherwise use an opaque surface.
Provide a solid fill when the person has asked for reduced transparency.
On the web, use backdrop-filter sparingly and always set an opaque background as the fallback.

cssNotes: A bar can use background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-bg) 80%, transparent) and backdrop-filter: blur(20px).
Under @media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce), drop the blur and use var(--color-bg-elevated).
Do not stack multiple backdrop-filter layers.
accessibility: Text on a translucent surface still meets contrast against the worst-case content behind it.
Honor prefers-reduced-transparency.

title: Motion
summary: Motion explains what changed, where something went, or that work is still happening.
whenToUse: To show a panel arriving from the control that opened it.
To indicate progress when a result is not instant.
whenNotToUse: To animate essential text so it can be missed.
As a looping decoration on content people are trying to read.

rules.statement: Prefer short opacity and transform changes over large movements.
A transition should connect the control people used with the surface that appeared.
When reduced motion is on, replace movement with a fade or an instant change.
On the web, keep most transitions under a few hundred milliseconds and disable them under prefers-reduced-motion.

cssNotes: transition: opacity 180ms ease, transform 180ms ease.
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { transition: none; }
Do not animate layout properties such as height on large regions.
accessibility: Nothing important depends on seeing the animation.
Honor prefers-reduced-motion.

title: Accessibility
summary: Every control needs a name, a comfortable target, and a way to work without color, sound, or a precise pointer.
whenToUse: On every interactive control and image that carries meaning.
When reviewing contrast, focus, and text size before shipping.
whenNotToUse: As a mode that removes features people still need.

rules.statement: Give every control an accessible name that states the action, not the icon shape.
Keep a hit region of at least 44 by 44 points, and leave space between adjacent targets.
Do not use color alone for status, selection, or errors.
Support larger text without clipping or overlapping controls.
On the web, expose name, role, and state to the accessibility tree and provide a visible keyboard focus.

cssNotes: :focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--color-accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
Minimum control size: min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px.
Prefer native elements so role and keyboard behavior come for free.
accessibility: Icon-only buttons need aria-label or visually hidden text.
State changes that are not focus moves use an aria-live region sparingly.

title: Dark Mode
summary: Design light and dark as two appearances of the same hierarchy, not as an inverted screenshot.
whenToUse: Whenever the product has a light appearance.
When elevated sheets and bars need to stay distinct from the base background.
whenNotToUse: To invert brand artwork, photos, or logos.

rules.statement: Keep the same roles in both appearances and change the values, not the structure.
In dark appearance, raised surfaces can be slightly lighter than the base background.
Check text, separators, and the accent color on both appearances.
On the web, follow prefers-color-scheme unless the person has chosen an appearance in the product.

cssNotes: color-scheme: light dark on the document.
Override the same custom properties inside @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark).
If you offer a manual theme, set data-theme on the root and do not fight the system choice without a control.
accessibility: Contrast targets apply in both appearances.
Do not flash a light theme before the dark theme loads.

title: Writing
summary: Interface copy names the action, stays short, and tells people what to do next when something fails.
whenToUse: On buttons, empty states, errors, and permission explanations.
When a symbol is not universally understood.
whenNotToUse: To add a greeting or joke inside an alert.
To describe the control type, as in 'Click the button below'.

rules.statement: Start button labels with a verb and keep them to a few words, such as Add to Cart.
An error says what happened and how to fix it, without blaming the person.
Use the same term for the same object throughout the product.
On the web, the visible label and the accessible name should match.

cssNotes: Keep button text on one line when you can. Allow wrapping instead of shrinking the type size.
Place helper text under the field it describes, in the secondary label color.
accessibility: Do not put essential instructions only in placeholder text.
Error text is linked to the field with aria-describedby.

title: Right to left
summary: Mirror the layout for right-to-left languages. Leave numbers, brand marks, and directional media as they are.
whenToUse: When the product supports Arabic, Hebrew, or another right-to-left language.
whenNotToUse: To flip photographs, playback controls that represent time, or a logo that has a fixed direction.

rules.statement: Mirror navigation, alignment, and the position of the primary action.
Keep phone numbers, clocks, and media timelines in their natural direction.
On the web, set dir on the document and use logical properties such as margin-inline and padding-inline.

cssNotes: Use margin-inline, padding-inline, inset-inline, and text-align: start.
Flex and grid with logical properties mirror without a separate stylesheet.
Set dir='rtl' from the locale, not from a CSS hack.
accessibility: The accessibility tree follows the document direction.
Icons that mean forward or back should mirror; icons that depict an object should not.

title: Icons
summary: An icon stands for one familiar action. When the meaning is not obvious, add a label.
whenToUse: For a standard action such as share, search, close, or add.
Beside a short label in a toolbar or tab.
whenNotToUse: As the only label for a novel or destructive action.
To ship Apple's SF Symbols artwork in a product that is not licensed to do so.

rules.statement: Use one symbol per action and keep the same symbol for that action everywhere.
Cite an SF Symbol by name, such as square.and.arrow.up for share, without embedding the symbol artwork.
Add a text label when the symbol is not a common action.
On the web, use an icon set you have a license for, and give icon-only buttons an accessible name.

cssNotes: Size icons on the text grid, often 20 or 24 pixels, and align them to the label cap height.
Use currentColor so icons follow the label color in both appearances.
Do not hotlink Apple's HIG artwork or bundle SF Symbols.
accessibility: Decorative icons are aria-hidden. Meaningful icons have a text alternative.
The accessible name matches the visible label when both are present.

title: Buttons
summary: A button performs an immediate action. Style shows which action is preferred; the label says what it does.
whenToUse: For an action that happens as soon as the control is activated.
To offer one preferred action and a quieter alternative.
whenNotToUse: To open a list of commands. Use a menu.
To switch a setting that takes effect immediately. Use a toggle.

rules.statement: Use at most one or two prominent buttons in a view.
Distinguish the preferred action with prominence, not with a different size.
Roles are normal, primary, cancel, and destructive. Do not give the primary role to an action that destroys data.
Show a pressed state, and keep the hit region at least 44 by 44 points.
Label the button with a short verb in title case.
On visionOS, prefer a visible background shape and keep button centers at least 60 points apart.
On watchOS, a primary action can span the width of the screen.
On the web, use a button element. A primary button uses the accent fill. A destructive button uses the danger color and asks for confirmation when data would be lost.

cssNotes: button { min-height: 44px; padding-inline: 16px; border-radius: 8px; font: inherit; }
Primary: background var(--color-accent), label in a contrasting color. Secondary: transparent or elevated fill with an accent label.
type=submit inside a form. type=button everywhere else. Do not use a clickable div.
accessibility: The accessible name is the visible label.
Disabled buttons stay in the tab order only if you explain why they are unavailable; otherwise remove the action.

title: Text fields
summary: A text field collects a short value. The label says what to enter, and the field type matches the data.
whenToUse: For a name, email, search query, or other short value the person must type.
whenNotToUse: For a value chosen from a known set. Use a picker.
For a paragraph of text. Use a text view.

rules.statement: Put a visible label with the field. Placeholder text is a hint, not the label.
Choose the most specific input type, such as email or password.
Keep the person's text when validation fails, and explain the fix next to the field.
On the web, connect the label with for/id, set autocomplete, and point aria-describedby at the error.

cssNotes: Place the label above the field. The field uses the body type size so mobile browsers do not zoom on focus.
input { min-height: 44px; width: 100%; font: inherit; background: var(--color-bg-elevated); color: var(--color-label); }
Mark aria-invalid when the value is wrong.
accessibility: Every field has a label element or aria-label.
Password fields can be revealed without removing the secure default.

title: Toggles
summary: A toggle changes a setting immediately. The label names the outcome that is on.
whenToUse: For a setting that takes effect as soon as it changes, such as Face ID or notifications.
whenNotToUse: For a choice that is saved with a separate submit button. Use a checkbox.
For several mutually exclusive options. Use a segmented control or picker.

rules.statement: The change applies immediately. Do not also require a Save button for that single setting.
Label the outcome, such as Notifications, rather than the words On and Off alone.
On the web, use a switch semantics and expose the checked state.

cssNotes: input[type=checkbox][role=switch], or a button with aria-pressed when the control is custom.
The label is beside the switch, and the whole row meets 44 pixels.
Do not rely on green and gray alone. The position and aria-checked carry the state.
accessibility: role=switch and aria-checked=true or false.
The accessible name is the setting label.

title: Segmented controls
summary: A segmented control shows a few mutually exclusive choices that all stay visible.
whenToUse: For two to five options that filter or change the current view.
whenNotToUse: For top-level navigation between unrelated areas. Use tabs or a sidebar.
For a long list of choices. Use a picker.

rules.statement: Keep every option visible and similar in length.
Selection changes the content in place. It does not push a new screen.
On the web, use a radiogroup when the control changes a setting, and a tablist only when each segment shows a panel.

cssNotes: Lay segments in one row with an equal flex share. The selected segment uses the accent fill.
Wrap to a select only if the labels cannot fit without shrinking below body size.
The group has an accessible name.
accessibility: Arrow keys move between segments. The selected segment exposes aria-checked or aria-selected.
Do not use this pattern for site navigation.

title: Pickers
summary: A picker chooses from a known set so people do not have to type a value the product already understands.
whenToUse: For a date, a quantity, or a short list of valid values.
whenNotToUse: For free text such as a name.
For two simple options that fit on screen. Use a segmented control.

rules.statement: Show the current value in the closed control.
Order options in a way people expect, such as chronological or alphabetical, and include only valid choices.
On the web, use a native select for a short list and a dialog or listbox when the list is long or needs search.

cssNotes: Native select keeps the platform picker, including date and number wheels where the browser provides them.
A custom listbox is a button that shows the value plus a listbox anchored to it.
min-height: 44px on the closed control.
accessibility: The closed control's name includes the field label and the current value.
A custom listbox supports arrow keys, type-ahead, and Escape.

title: Lists and tables
summary: A list is a column of items with one primary label. A table is for data that is compared across columns.
whenToUse: To present many items of the same kind.
To compare values down a column.
whenNotToUse: For a handful of settings that are not a repeating item. A grouped form is enough.
For a data table when each row is really navigation.

rules.statement: Give each row one primary label. Put secondary details in a quieter style.
A row that navigates should look like it navigates, with a disclosure or a link.
Put frequent row actions in a small set of buttons or a swipe action. Put the rest in a menu.
On the web, use a list for navigation and a table only when the content is tabular data.

cssNotes: Rows are at least 44 pixels tall. Separate them with a hairline using --color-separator.
A navigation row is an a or button that fills the row, not a click handler on a div.
Tables get a caption or an accessible name, and headers use th scope.
accessibility: List rows that are links expose the destination in the name.
Sortable columns expose sort state.

title: Tab bars
summary: A tab bar holds a few stable top-level destinations.
whenToUse: For three to five areas people switch between often on a narrow screen.
whenNotToUse: For more destinations than fit comfortably. Use a sidebar.
For filters inside one screen. Use a segmented control.

rules.statement: Keep the tab bar stable. Do not change its items as people move within a section.
Each tab has a short label and, when you use a symbol, the same symbol every time.
On a wide web layout, replace a bottom tab bar with a sidebar.
Mark the selected tab.

cssNotes: nav { display: flex; } with an a for each destination and aria-current=page on the active one.
On narrow screens, position the nav at the bottom with padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom).
At wider widths, move the same links into a sidebar. Do not show both.
accessibility: The landmark is named, for example aria-label=Primary.
The current page is aria-current=page, not color alone.

title: Sidebars
summary: A sidebar lists many destinations or a source list beside a detail pane.
whenToUse: When there are more sections than a tab bar can hold.
When people need to keep a list and a detail on screen together.
whenNotToUse: On a narrow phone layout where a tab bar or a single stack is clearer.
For commands that act on the current view. Use a toolbar or menu.

rules.statement: The sidebar selects a destination. It does not perform a one-off command.
On a narrow width, collapse the sidebar behind a control instead of squeezing the detail.
Show which item is selected.

cssNotes: A two-column grid: sidebar around 240 to 280 pixels, detail in the remaining space.
Below about 800 pixels, hide the sidebar and open it from a button as a dialog or disclosure.
Selected item uses accent text or a quiet fill plus aria-current.
accessibility: nav aria-label describes the sidebar.
When collapsed into a dialog, focus moves into it and returns to the button that opened it.

title: Toolbars
summary: A toolbar holds actions for the current view, with the title in the middle or leading side and the main action at the trailing side.
whenToUse: For actions that apply to the screen people are looking at.
For a back control and a title.
whenNotToUse: For top-level navigation between sections. Use a tab bar or sidebar.
For a long list of rare commands. Use a menu.

rules.statement: Toolbar items act on the current view.
Place the primary action at the trailing end in left-to-right layouts.
Icon-only items need a tooltip and an accessible name.
On the web, the toolbar is a header, and every item is a button or a link.

cssNotes: header { display: flex; align-items: center; min-height: 44px; gap: 8px; }
The title is an h1 for the screen. Actions sit in a group at the end.
A translucent bar can use the materials guidance, with a solid fallback.
accessibility: Icon buttons have aria-label.
The header does not trap keyboard focus.

title: Search fields
summary: A search field finds content. It shows the query and offers a way to clear it.
whenToUse: When a list is long enough that scrolling is a poor way to find an item.
whenNotToUse: On a short list people can scan.
As the only navigation through the product.

rules.statement: Show the current query and a clear control once there is text.
Say what the field searches when the scope is not obvious.
On the web, use input type=search inside a search landmark, with a visible label.

cssNotes: form role=search, or a search element, containing label and input type=search.
The clear control is a button with an accessible name, shown only when the field has a value.
Results replace or filter the list below. Do not navigate away on each keystroke.
accessibility: The input has a label such as Search.
If results update live, mark the results region aria-live=polite only when the update is infrequent enough to be useful.

title: Menus
summary: A menu lists commands related to a control or the current selection.
whenToUse: For secondary commands that do not fit in the toolbar.
For actions on a selected item.
whenNotToUse: For navigation to another section of the product. Use a sidebar or tabs.
For a single primary action. Use a button.

rules.statement: Menu items are commands. Keep destructive commands last and label them clearly.
Use a few items with short labels. Group related commands.
On the web, the menu opens from a button, closes on Escape or outside click, and supports arrow keys.

cssNotes: button aria-haspopup=menu aria-expanded, controlling a menu element positioned at the button.
Items are menuitem buttons. A danger item uses --color-danger for its label.
Prefer the popover API or a positioned list. Do not use a native select for commands.
accessibility: Arrow keys move, Enter activates, Escape closes and returns focus to the button.
Disabled commands remain visible when people need to know they exist, and expose aria-disabled.

title: Sheets
summary: A sheet is a short task that appears above the current view and returns people there when it is done.
whenToUse: For a focused task such as composing, filtering, or confirming a purchase.
When the parent screen should stay in context.
whenNotToUse: For a long multi-step flow. Use a full screen.
For a critical irreversible decision with no other content. Use an alert.

rules.statement: Give the sheet a title, a way to dismiss it, and a primary action when the task has one.
Do not stack sheets. Finish or dismiss the current one first.
On a small web viewport, a sheet can use the full height. On a wide viewport, keep it a dialog anchored to the task.

cssNotes: dialog.showModal() with a form inside. The primary button is type=submit. Cancel is type=button and calls close().
On narrow screens, dialog { width: 100%; height: 100%; max-height: 100%; margin: 0; }.
On wide screens, max-width around 32rem and a radius. Use the materials guidance only for a non-modal panel.
accessibility: Focus moves into the dialog and returns to the opener on close.
aria-labelledby points at the sheet title. Escape dismisses when dismissal is safe.

title: Alerts
summary: An alert interrupts for a problem or a decision people need to handle before they continue.
whenToUse: To confirm a destructive action.
To report a problem that blocks the current task.
whenNotToUse: To celebrate success. Use inline feedback.
To ask for a permission before the person understands why.

rules.statement: Show one alert at a time. The title is the situation, the message is the consequence, and the buttons are actions.
The default button is the safe action. A destructive action is not the default.
Use at most a few buttons, each with a specific verb rather than Yes and No when you can be specific.
On the web, use an alertdialog, not window.alert, so the title, message, and actions follow this structure.

cssNotes: dialog role=alertdialog, a short h2, one paragraph, and a button row.
The safe action comes last in left-to-right reading order so it sits at the trailing edge, and it receives initial focus when the choice is risky.
The destructive button uses --color-danger and is not type=submit by default.
accessibility: aria-labelledby and aria-describedby point at the title and message.
Focus is trapped until the person chooses an action.

title: Popovers
summary: A popover is a small surface anchored to the control that opened it.
whenToUse: For a short piece of related content or a small set of options tied to one control.
whenNotToUse: For a task with several fields. Use a sheet.
For information people must not miss. Do not hide required content in a popover.

rules.statement: Anchor the popover to the control that opened it, and point it at that control.
Dismiss it when people activate outside it or press Escape.
On a narrow web layout, prefer a sheet if the popover cannot fit.

cssNotes: button aria-expanded controls an element using the popover API, positioned next to the button.
Keep the popover within the viewport. If it cannot, use a dialog sheet instead.
Padding at least 12 pixels, type at body or callout size.
accessibility: Focus can move into the popover. Escape returns focus to the button.
Hover-only tooltips are not the only way to read the content. Focus shows them too.

title: Progress indicators
summary: Show determinate progress when you know how much work remains. Use an indeterminate indicator when you do not.
whenToUse: While a request, upload, or other wait is visible.
Inside a button when that button's action is in flight.
whenNotToUse: For a wait so short that the indicator would flash.
As a full-screen block when part of the content is already ready.

rules.statement: Use a determinate bar when the fraction remaining is known. Use a spinner when it is not.
A busy button can replace its icon with a spinner and change its label, such as from Save to Saving.
On the web, pair the indicator with text. A spinner alone is not the status.

cssNotes: progress for a known value. An indeterminate wait can be a status element with a CSS spinner.
If the button is busy, set aria-busy and disabled on that button only.
Reserve the indicator's space so the layout does not jump.
accessibility: progress has a label. Determinate progress exposes the value.
Honor prefers-reduced-motion by reducing or removing the spin.

title: Onboarding
summary: Onboarding gets people to the first useful task quickly and asks only for what that task needs.
whenToUse: When the first screen would otherwise be empty or unclear.
When a permission is required for the feature the person just chose.
whenNotToUse: To present a tour of every feature.
To ask for an account, notifications, and location before any value is shown.

rules.statement: Lead with the task, not a carousel of marketing pages.
Request a permission in context, after the person has asked for the feature that needs it.
Offer a way to skip optional setup.
On the web, keep first-run steps on one route people can leave, and do not request notification permission on load.

cssNotes: One primary button for the next step. A quiet text button for Skip.
Do not autoplay a tour. If you show steps, show the step count.
Store completion locally so the intro does not repeat.
accessibility: The step heading is the page heading.
Skip is a real button, not a timed dismissal.

title: Modality
summary: Modality pauses the parent view for a task or decision that people should finish or explicitly dismiss.
whenToUse: When continuing underneath would lose data or make the choice ambiguous.
whenNotToUse: For content people may want to compare with the parent.
To stack a second modal on the first.

rules.statement: Use a sheet for a task and an alert for a decision.
Always offer an explicit dismiss or cancel path.
Do not open a modal on top of another modal.
On the web, a modal dialog traps focus and returns it to the control that opened it.

cssNotes: Use the dialog element with showModal so the browser provides the top layer and inert background.
The backdrop is a dimmer, not another blurred stack.
Closing restores focus.
accessibility: The element behind the dialog is inert.
Escape closes a sheet. An alert closes only from its actions when the choice is required.

title: Entering data
summary: Ask for the smallest amount of information, with the control that makes mistakes unlikely.
whenToUse: For a form, checkout, or any screen that collects values.
whenNotToUse: To ask for data you already have or do not need for the task.

rules.statement: Pick the control that matches the data: field, picker, toggle, or stepper.
Validate when the person leaves a field or submits, and keep what they typed.
Put the error next to the field and say how to fix it.
On the web, turn on autocomplete for names, addresses, and payment details the browser can fill.

cssNotes: One column on narrow screens. Labels above fields. Related fields in a fieldset with a legend.
The submit button states the outcome, such as Place Order, and shows a busy state while the request runs.
novalidate only if you replace the browser's messages with your own, still tied to each field.
accessibility: Errors use aria-invalid and aria-describedby.
A form-level error summary moves focus to the summary and links to each field.

title: Feedback
summary: Feedback tells people what happened and what they can do next, close to the action that caused it.
whenToUse: After a save, a failed request, or an empty result.
To show progress while work continues.
whenNotToUse: As an alert for ordinary success.
As a message that disappears before it can be read.

rules.statement: Confirm a meaningful result near the action. Do not send people to another screen just to say it worked.
An error names the problem and the next step.
An empty state explains why it is empty and offers the action that fills it.
On the web, a transient status can use a polite live region. A problem that needs a decision uses an alert.

cssNotes: Place success or error text directly under the control or at the top of the form.
Empty states sit in the content region: one sentence, then a primary button.
Do not rely on a toast as the only copy of an error.
accessibility: role=status for non-critical updates.
Errors that block progress are linked from an error summary.

title: Loading
summary: Show content as soon as it exists. Indicate waiting only when the person would otherwise wonder if the product stalled.
whenToUse: When a screen or a region cannot render its real content yet.
whenNotToUse: To block the whole product for a request that only affects one region.
For a delay so short the indicator flashes.

rules.statement: Prefer showing the shell of the screen and filling it in to blocking on a blank page.
Use determinate progress when you know the fraction remaining.
On the web, reserve the space of the content that is loading so the page does not jump.

cssNotes: A skeleton uses the same layout as the loaded content and a quiet elevated fill.
Set aria-busy on the region that is loading, not on the whole document, once the first content is visible.
Do not animate a skeleton when prefers-reduced-motion is set.
accessibility: The loading region has an accessible name such as Loading articles.
When content arrives, do not move focus unless the person was waiting on that result.

title: Searching
summary: Search tells people what scope it covers, keeps the query visible, and helps when nothing matches.
whenToUse: To find an item in a long collection or across the product.
whenNotToUse: To hide poor organization of a small set of items.

rules.statement: State the scope, such as this mailbox or the whole library, when more than one scope exists.
Keep the query visible while results are showing.
An empty result suggests a next step, such as clearing a filter or checking the spelling.
On the web, reflect the query in the URL when the result is a destination people might share or revisit.

cssNotes: The field stays above the results. Filters are chips or a menu, not a second hidden form.
Highlighting the match is optional and never the only way to see why a row matched.
Use the search field card for the control itself.
accessibility: Results are a list or a live region with a count people can find, such as 12 results.
Clear search is a button.

title: Settings
summary: Settings change how the product behaves. The product should still make sense if a person never opens them.
whenToUse: For choices that persist, such as appearance, notifications, or account details.
whenNotToUse: As a second home for primary features.
For a value that only applies to the current task. Keep that next to the task.

rules.statement: Choose safe, useful defaults so settings are optional.
Group related settings and put infrequent or destructive ones farther down.
A setting's label names the outcome. Helper text explains the consequence when it is not obvious.
On the web, a settings screen is a grouped list of labeled controls, not a wall of unlabeled inputs.

cssNotes: Group with fieldset and legend, or with h2 headings and lists.
Toggles apply immediately. Fields that are edited together can share a Save button in the toolbar.
Destructive account actions sit in their own group at the end and require confirmation.
accessibility: Each control has a visible label.
Helper text is tied to the control with aria-describedby.

title: Managing accounts
summary: An account should unlock something people already want, and signing out or deleting it should be easy to find.
whenToUse: When the product stores personal data or syncs across devices.
whenNotToUse: Before people have seen why an account helps.
As a gate on content that does not need an identity.

rules.statement: Explain what the account unlocks before asking people to create one.
If you offer third-party sign-in on an Apple platform, also offer Sign in with Apple.
Put sign-out and account deletion where people manage the account, and confirm deletion.
On the web, keep the signed-in state visible and do not hide account deletion.

cssNotes: Sign-in offers the same providers you show elsewhere, with clear button labels.
The account screen repeats the identity, then settings, then sign out, then delete account.
Deletion uses the alert pattern and requires an explicit confirm.
accessibility: Password fields have autocomplete=current-password or new-password.
Errors from a failed sign-in are text, not only a color on the field.

title: Managing notifications
summary: Ask for notification permission after the benefit is clear, and let people reduce notifications later.
whenToUse: When a timely event happens that the person asked to hear about.
whenNotToUse: At first launch.
For marketing that is not time sensitive.

rules.statement: Request permission in context, after people understand what they will be told.
Every notification should be timely and actionable.
Offer in-product controls to quiet categories or turn notifications off.
On the web, do not call Notification.requestPermission on load.

cssNotes: A button such as Notify me starts the browser permission prompt after a sentence that says what will be sent.
Settings list each category with a toggle.
If permission is denied, explain how to turn it back on in the browser instead of asking in a loop.
accessibility: The pre-prompt is text plus a button, not a surprise dialog.
Category toggles follow the toggle card.
